questions.q: Total body water (TBW) in infants is approximately what percentage of body weight?
questions.e: TBW declines with age: it is about 73% of body weight in infants, roughly 60% in adults, and can fall as low as 45% in old age.

questions.q: Total body water (TBW) in adults is approximately what percentage of body weight?
questions.e: TBW is about 60% of body weight in adults, down from ≈73% in infancy.

questions.q: In old age, TBW can decline to as low as:
questions.e: TBW continues to decline with age and can be as low as 45% of body weight in old age.

questions.q: TBW correlates inversely with which body characteristic?
questions.e: TBW correlates inversely with body fat because adipose (fat) tissue is the least hydrated tissue in the body.

questions.q: In men, TBW is approximately what percentage of body weight?
questions.e: TBW in men is about 55–60% of body weight, higher than in young women due to differences in body composition.

questions.q: In young women, TBW is approximately what percentage of body weight?
questions.e: TBW in young women is about 45–50% of body weight — lower than in men, largely reflecting a higher proportion of adipose tissue.

questions.q: The percentage of water in fat-free tissue (lean body mass) is remarkably constant at approximately:
questions.e: Despite variation in overall TBW with age, sex, and adiposity, the water content of lean body mass stays remarkably constant at about 73%.

questions.q: In steady state, total body water is estimated to vary by less than what percentage over 24 hours?
questions.e: The body maintains tight constancy in water content — TBW varies by less than 1% over 24 hours in steady state.

questions.q: In steady state, the relationship between water intake and water loss is best described as:
questions.e: Water balance is controlled by regulating intake and loss; in steady state, water intake equals water loss.

questions.q: Intracellular fluid (ICF) comprises what fraction of total body water?
questions.e: ICF comprises about 2/3 of TBW, found within the cells of the body.

questions.q: ICF constitutes approximately what percentage of total body weight?
questions.e: ICF constitutes about 40% of body weight.

questions.q: Extracellular fluid (ECF) comprises what fraction of total body water?
questions.e: ECF comprises the remaining 1/3 of TBW, found outside the cells.

questions.q: ECF constitutes approximately what percentage of total body weight?
questions.e: ECF constitutes about 20% of body weight.

questions.q: Which ionic profile best characterizes intracellular fluid (ICF)?
o: High Ca²⁺, with all other ions absent
High K⁺ and Mg²⁺; low Na⁺ and Cl⁻
Equal concentrations of Na⁺ and K⁺
High Na⁺ and Cl⁻; low K⁺ and Mg²⁺
questions.e: ICF is high in potassium, magnesium, phosphate, organic anions, and proteins, and low in sodium, bicarbonate, and chloride.

questions.q: Which ionic profile best characterizes extracellular fluid (ECF)?
o: Low K⁺ and Mg²⁺; high Na⁺, Cl⁻, and HCO₃⁻
Equal concentrations of all major ions
High phosphate and organic anions only
High K⁺ and Mg²⁺; low Na⁺ and Cl⁻
questions.e: ECF is low in potassium and magnesium ions, and high in sodium, chloride, and bicarbonate ions.

questions.q: Interstitial fluid (ISF) comprises approximately what fraction of the ECF?
questions.e: ISF comprises about 3/4 of the ECF; it surrounds the cells but does not circulate.

questions.q: Which one of these cannot be measured directly using a marker?
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. There is no marker that distributes only in the interstitial space; it is calculated indirectly as ECF volume minus plasma volume.

questions.q: Plasma makes up approximately what fraction of the ECF?
questions.e: Plasma, which circulates as the extracellular component of blood, makes up about 1/4 of the ECF.

questions.q: Approximately how large is the transcellular fluid compartment?
questions.e: Transcellular fluid comprises a very small portion of TBW, about 0.5 to 2 liters, contained within epithelial-lined spaces.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT classified as a transcellular fluid?
questions.e: Plasma is a separate ECF subcompartment; transcellular fluids include CSF, GIT fluids, serous fluid, aqueous humor, and joint, peritoneal, and pericardial fluids.

questions.q: According to the composition table, plasma Na⁺ concentration is approximately:
questions.e: Plasma Na⁺ concentration is approximately 143 mmol/L, much higher than the ICF value of about 9 mmol/L.

questions.q: According to the composition table, ICF K⁺ concentration is approximately:
questions.e: ICF K⁺ concentration is approximately 135 mmol/L, much higher than the plasma value of about 5 mmol/L.

questions.q: Which one of these is not true about plasma membranes?
o: It is involved in cell to cell communication
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. The lipid bilayer is actually poorly permeable to ions; ions cross mainly through specific channels/transporters, not by free diffusion.

questions.q: If 30 mg of glucose is added to an unknown volume of distilled water and the final concentration of glucose after mixing is 0.10 mg/ml, then the volume of solvent is?
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Volume = mass ÷ concentration = 30 mg ÷ 0.10 mg/ml = 300 ml.

questions.q: What type of lipids are the most abundant in the cell membrane?
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Phospholipids form the structural backbone of the membrane (the bilayer itself) and are by far the most abundant lipid class. Cholesterol is present in smaller amounts (modulating fluidity) and glycolipids make up an even smaller fraction, confined to the outer leaflet.

questions.q: In the plasma membrane, carbohydrates:
o: Always face outward, towards extracellular space
Always face inward, towards the non-polar portion of the membrane
Are directed to all sides in the membrane
Always face the lumen of the cell
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Membrane carbohydrates are attached to lipids (glycolipids) or proteins (glycoproteins) exclusively on the outer leaflet, forming the glycocalyx. This layer faces the extracellular space and is involved in cell recognition, adhesion, and protection — it never faces the cytoplasmic side.

questions.q: The main component of the lipid bilayer is:
questions.e: Phospholipids are the main components of the lipid bilayer, with hydrophilic phosphate heads and hydrophobic fatty-acid tails.

questions.q: In the phospholipid bilayer, the hydrophobic fatty-acid tails:
o: Align next to and opposite each other, facing inward
questions.e: Hydrophobic tails align next to and opposite each other, forming a bilayer core, while hydrophilic heads point outward toward the aqueous environment.

questions.q: T-tubules are contiguous with which membrane system?
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. T-tubules (transverse tubules) are tube-like invaginations of the sarcolemma (the muscle cell membrane) that dive deep into the fiber, allowing the action potential to reach the interior of the cell rapidly and uniformly.

questions.q: The least phospholipids present in the plasma membranes are the
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Phosphatidylcholine is the most abundant membrane phospholipid; phosphatidylinositol is present in the smallest amount, though it is functionally important as a second-messenger precursor.

questions.q: Cholesterol reduces membrane fluidity mainly by:
questions.e: Cholesterol reduces membrane fluidity by reducing the movement of phospholipid molecules, while also providing mechanical stability.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT listed as a function of cholesterol in the membrane?
o: Decreases permeability to small water-soluble molecules
Lowers the temperature needed for the membrane to solidify
questions.e: Cholesterol provides mechanical stability, decreases permeability to small water-soluble molecules, and lowers the solidification temperature — it does not generate ATP.

questions.q: Integral membrane proteins with hydrophobic regions that completely span the membrane, exposing hydrophilic ends on both sides, are called:
questions.e: Transmembrane proteins are integral proteins that span the entire hydrophobic interior of the membrane, with hydrophilic ends exposed to solutions on both sides.

questions.q: Regarding the cell membrane, which of the following is FALSE?
o: About 50% of the cell membrane is made up of protein
The proteins of the cell membrane function as channels, carriers, enzymes and receptors
The membrane's fluidity is increased by unsaturated fatty acid tails in the phospholipids
The hydrophilic part of the cell membrane is at the interior side of the cell membrane
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. The membrane is a phospholipid bilayer: the hydrophilic (polar) heads face outward on BOTH surfaces (toward the extracellular fluid and toward the cytoplasm), while the hydrophobic tails point inward, forming the membrane's non-polar core. Saying the hydrophilic part is only 'at the interior side' is incorrect — that describes the hydrophobic tails, not the heads. (Note: option D was left incomplete in the original paper and has been reconstructed here as a true statement to complete the option set.)

questions.q: Peripheral membrane proteins differ from integral proteins in that they:
o: Cannot interact with the membrane at all
Are not embedded in the lipid bilayer, sitting on the membrane surface
Are embedded in the lipid bilayer
questions.e: Peripheral proteins are not embedded in the lipid bilayer; they sit on the membrane surface, held by ionic and hydrogen-bond interactions.

questions.q: Which one of these is not true about transmembrane proteins?
o: They can be removed by alkaline solutions
They are embedded in the lipid bilayer
They have both hydrophobic and hydrophilic ends
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Integral/transmembrane proteins span the bilayer and need detergents to be removed. Alkaline (or high salt) solutions only strip loosely-associated peripheral proteins.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT listed as a function of plasma membrane proteins?
o: Cell adhesion molecules and gap junctions
questions.e: Membrane proteins function as channels, carriers, receptors, enzymes, cell adhesion molecules, gap junctions, desmosomes, tight junctions, antigens, surface recognition molecules, and cytoskeleton contacts — not as direct ATP generators.

questions.q: Which of these membrane transport processes does not exhibit a saturation limit?
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Simple/ionic diffusion through channels or the lipid bilayer is not carrier-mediated, so it does not saturate. All carrier-mediated processes (active transport, facilitated diffusion) do saturate.

questions.q: Diffusion is best defined as:
o: Active pumping of molecules against a gradient
Random thermal motion of molecules resulting in net flux toward lower concentration
questions.e: Diffusion is the random thermal motion of molecules that results in a net flux toward regions of lower concentration, moving the system toward equilibrium.

questions.q: The time required to reach diffusion equilibrium is proportionate to:
o: The square of the diffusion distance
The cube root of the diffusion distance
questions.e: Time required for equilibrium by diffusion is proportionate to the square of the diffusion distance.

questions.q: Simple diffusion is defined as a substance passing through a membrane:
o: With the aid of a carrier protein that changes shape
Without the aid of an intermediary such as an integral membrane protein
questions.e: Simple diffusion refers to a substance passing through the membrane without the aid of an intermediary such as an integral membrane protein.

questions.q: Which substances cross cell membranes more readily by simple diffusion?
questions.e: Lipid or non-polar soluble substances cross cell membranes more readily by simple diffusion than water-soluble substances do.

questions.q: Osmosis always involves
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Osmosis is the diffusion of solvent (water) across a semipermeable membrane down its concentration gradient — so it involves all three: a membrane, a concentration difference, and diffusion.

questions.q: According to Fick's first law, diffusive flux across a membrane is directly proportional to which of the following?
o: Concentration difference, surface area, and diffusion coefficient
questions.e: Fick's first law states diffusive flux is directly proportional to the concentration difference across the membrane, the surface area, and the diffusion coefficient.

questions.q: Which one of these is not true about Fick's first law of diffusion?
o: Diffusion rate is directly proportional to concentration gradient of the substance across the membrane
Diffusion rate is directly proportional to thickness of the membrane
Diffusion rate is directly proportional to diffusion coefficient
Diffusion rate is directly proportional to surface area of the membrane
Diffusion rate is directly proportional to permeability of the membrane to the substance
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Fick's law: rate is inversely proportional to membrane thickness (the thicker the membrane, the slower the diffusion) — not directly proportional.

questions.q: Fick's first law of diffusion applies to systems that are:
o: At steady state, where concentration remains constant
questions.e: Fick's first law applies to steady-state systems, where concentration keeps constant over time.

questions.q: Membrane junctions that allow nutrients or ions to flow from cell to cell are
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Gap junctions are made of connexons that form direct cytoplasmic channels between adjacent cells, allowing ions/small molecules to pass.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the gating types listed for ion channels?
questions.e: Gated ion channels are described as voltage-gated, ligand (chemical)-gated, or mechanically-gated. Temperature-gated channels are not among the types listed here.

questions.q: The net transmembrane flux of an ion is proportional to the combined effect of:
o: Both the electrical and concentration gradients
questions.e: Ionic movement is affected by electrical charge as well as concentration — the net transmembrane flux of an ion is proportional to the combined electrical and chemical gradients, i.e. the electrochemical gradient.

questions.q: In active transport, substances are moved:
questions.e: In active transport, substances are moved against their electrochemical gradient, requiring a carrier protein and energy.

questions.q: Active transport requires which two things that facilitated diffusion does not?
questions.e: Unlike facilitated diffusion, active transport requires both a carrier protein and metabolic energy, since it moves substances against their gradient.

questions.q: The most important factor in decreasing the intracellular Ca2+ concentration in skeletal muscle is
o: active transport of Ca2+ into the sarcoplasmic reticulum
active transport of Ca2+ into the synaptic cleft
diffusion of Ca2+ out of the cell
diffusion of Ca2+ into the sarcoplasm reticulum
active transport of Ca2+ across the sarcolemma
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. The SERCA pump actively transports Ca2+ back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum, which is the primary mechanism lowering cytosolic Ca2+ and allowing relaxation.

questions.q: Primary active transport utilizes metabolic energy directly in the form of:
questions.e: Primary active transport utilizes metabolic energy in the form of ATP directly, as with the Na⁺-K⁺ ATPase.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of primary active transport?
questions.e: Primary active transport pumps include the Na⁺-K⁺ ATPase, Ca²⁺ ATPase, and H⁺-K⁺ ATPase, which use ATP directly.

questions.q: Secondary active transport uses metabolic energy:
o: Not at all — it is purely passive
Directly, via ATP hydrolysis at the transporter itself
Indirectly, via energy stored in ion gradients established by primary active transport
questions.e: Secondary active transport is driven indirectly, using the free energy stored in ion gradients (established by primary active transport) rather than direct ATP hydrolysis.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of secondary active transport?
questions.e: Co-transport of Na⁺ with glucose (or amino acids) is a classic example of secondary active transport, coupled to the Na⁺ gradient generated by primary active transport.

questions.q: A membrane transport protein that moves only one kind of solute across the lipid bilayer is called a:
questions.e: Uniports move one kind of solute across the lipid bilayer, in contrast to cotransport systems that move two or more solutes.

questions.q: A cotransport system that sends two or more solutes in the SAME direction is called a:
questions.e: Symport systems are cotransport systems that send solutes in the same direction across the membrane.

questions.q: A cotransport system that sends solutes in OPPOSITE directions is called an:
questions.e: Antiport systems send solutes in opposite directions across the membrane — for example, the Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger.

questions.q: Vesicular transport involves the movement of macromolecules:
o: Within membrane-bound vesicles across cell membranes
questions.e: Vesicular transport involves the movement of macromolecules within membrane-bound vesicles across cell membranes.

questions.q: The two main types of vesicular transport are:
questions.e: The two main types of vesicular transport are endocytosis (uptake into the cell) and exocytosis (secretion out of the cell).

questions.q: During endocytosis, the protein responsible for pinching off the forming vesicle is:
questions.e: The molecule responsible for pinching off the vesicle during endocytosis is dynamin.

questions.q: Osmosis is best defined as:
o: Active pumping of water using ATP
Movement of ions through gated channels
Bulk fluid movement driven by hydrostatic pressure only
The passive diffusion of water across a semipermeable membrane from low to high solute concentration
questions.e: Osmosis is the passive diffusion of water across a semipermeable membrane from a region of low solute (high water) concentration to a region of high solute (low water) concentration.

questions.q: The presence of solute in a solution causes:
o: No change in the chemical potential of water
An increase in the chemical potential of water
A decrease in the chemical potential of water
questions.e: The presence of solute results in a decrease in the chemical potential of water, which drives osmotic water movement.

questions.q: Osmotic pressure is defined as:
o: The pressure difference driving simple diffusion
The pressure needed to force water through a membrane
The hydrostatic pressure required to stop the flow of water
The pressure exerted by gas molecules in solution
questions.e: Osmotic pressure is the hydrostatic pressure required to stop the flow of water across a semipermeable membrane.

questions.q: Osmotic pressure is primarily dependent on:
o: The number of particles in solution
The temperature of the membrane only
questions.e: Osmotic pressure is dependent on the number of particles in solution, regardless of what those particles are.

questions.q: If the total osmotic pressures of two solutions are equal, the solutions are said to be:
questions.e: If the total osmotic pressures of two solutions are equal, they are said to be isotonic to each other.

questions.q: If solution A has a greater osmotic pressure than solution B, solution A is said to be:
questions.e: If solution A has a greater osmotic pressure than solution B, A is described as hypertonic to B.

questions.q: If solution A has a lower osmotic pressure than solution B, solution A is said to be:
questions.e: If solution A has a lower osmotic pressure than solution B, A is described as hypotonic to B.

questions.q: ____ utilize aquaporins to rapidly move across cellular membranes
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Aquaporins are water-channel proteins that allow rapid, selective movement of water across the membrane.

questions.q: How is homeostasis best defined?
o: A one-time adjustment made at birth
The complete elimination of all internal fluctuations
The maintenance of a constant, relatively stable internal environment despite a changing external environment
The process by which cells divide and differentiate
questions.e: Homeostasis is the maintenance of a constant, relatively stable internal environment in the face of a changing external environment.

questions.q: Who proposed the principle of the constancy of the milieu intérieur, and in what year?
questions.e: Claude Bernard proposed the principle of the constancy of the milieu intérieur (internal environment) in 1878.

questions.q: According to Claude Bernard, why is the living body relatively independent of its external environment?
o: Because it has no need of the surrounding environment at all
Because its tissues are withdrawn from direct external influence and protected by the internal environment
Because it can survive without any fluids
Because external stimuli are filtered out by the skin alone
questions.e: Bernard explained that although the body needs its surroundings, its tissues are shielded from direct external influence by a true internal environment — the circulating body fluids.

questions.q: Who coined the term "homeostasis," and from what language are its roots derived?
questions.e: Walter Cannon coined the term homeostasis in 1932, from the Greek words homeo (same, similar) and stasis (standing, stillness).

questions.q: Which body fluid compartment is considered the "internal environment" in homeostasis?
questions.e: The extracellular fluid (ECF) is considered to be the internal environment that homeostatic mechanisms defend.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT listed among the essential variables of the internal environment?
o: Concentration of oxygen and carbon dioxide
Number of red blood cells produced per minute
Volume and pressure of extracellular fluid
questions.e: The essential variables include gas concentrations, pH, nutrient/waste levels, electrolyte concentration, ECF volume/pressure, and temperature — not a specific rate of red cell production.

questions.q: Concentration of salt and other electrolytes is regulated as part of which broader process?
questions.e: Electrolyte concentration is one of the essential variables of the internal environment kept within acceptable limits by homeostasis.

questions.q: A condition arising from disturbance of homeostasis is known as:
questions.e: Much disease results from disturbance of homeostasis, a condition known as homeostatic imbalance; understanding homeostasis underlies clinical diagnosis.

questions.q: Two of these organ systems bear the major responsibility for ensuring homeostasis: 1. Nervous system 2. Digestive system 3. Reproductive system 4. Cardiovascular system 5. Endocrine system
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. The nervous system and endocrine system are the two major regulatory systems that maintain homeostasis, communicating via electrical signals and hormones respectively.

questions.q: Homeostasis is credited with allowing humans to do what?
o: Bypass the need for nutrient intake
Live in a wide range of habitats
Eliminate the need for an immune system
questions.e: Homeostasis allows humans to live in many different habitats by keeping the internal environment stable despite external variation.

questions.q: What are the three components common to every homeostatic control system?
o: Detectors/sensors, an integrating/control center, and effectors
questions.e: Homeostatic control systems have three components: detectors/sensors, an integrating/control center, and effectors.

questions.q: Homeostatic control systems are subject to which two forms of regulation?
questions.e: Homeostatic control systems are subject to nervous and endocrine control.

questions.q: What are the two basic strategies the body uses to maintain homeostasis?
questions.e: Two basic strategies are used by the body to maintain homeostasis: feedback and feedforward.

questions.q: Feedback control can be classified into which two types?
questions.e: Feedback control can be either negative or positive.

questions.q: Which one of these is not controlled by negative feedback mechanism?
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. The pre-ovulatory LH surge is a classic example of positive feedback — rising estrogen further stimulates LH release rather than inhibiting it.

questions.q: Which statement about negative feedback is TRUE?
o: It always increases the deviation from set point
It is stimulatory and drives disequilibrium
Homeostasis primarily operates on this principle, and it is inhibitory
It is not involved in homeostasis at all
questions.e: Homeostasis primarily operates on the negative feedback principle; negative feedback responses are inhibitory and help maintain equilibrium.

questions.q: Positive feedback occurs when a change in a controlled variable triggers a response that:
o: Has a delayed but neutral effect
questions.e: Positive feedback occurs when a change in a controlled variable triggers a response that amplifies the change; it is stimulatory.

questions.q: Which of the following is TRUE of positive feedback?
o: It is the principal mechanism of homeostasis
It cannot ever assist negative feedback
It moves the controlled variable toward the set point and stabilizes it
It moves the controlled variable further from the set point and brings about disequilibrium
questions.e: Positive feedback moves the controlled variable further away from the set point, bringing about disequilibrium; it is not involved in homeostasis, though it can occasionally make negative feedback more efficient.

questions.q: The mechanism in which a response is generated in anticipation of a change in a control variable is
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Feedforward control anticipates a change and initiates a response before the change actually occurs (e.g. salivation at the sight of food).

questions.q: Unlike feedback control, feedforward control is:
questions.e: Feedforward control is not error-based; it prepares the body for a change in advance rather than correcting an already-occurred error.

questions.q: Which of these is a classic example of feedforward control?
o: Sweating in response to a rise in measured body temperature
Baroreceptor reflex correcting an already-fallen blood pressure
Shivering only once core temperature has already dropped
Insulin secretion triggered by the presence of food in the gut, before blood glucose rises
questions.e: Insulin secretion triggered by food in the gut anticipates the coming rise in blood glucose — a feedforward response, not a reaction to an error that has already occurred.

questions.q: Shivering that begins before a person actually dips into cold water is an example of:
questions.e: Shivering before dipping into cold water anticipates the coming cold stress, making it a feedforward response rather than a reaction to an already-occurred change.

questions.q: Signal transduction (cell signaling) is best defined as:
o: The physical division of one cell into two
The synthesis of DNA during the cell cycle
A cascade of processes converting an extracellular stimulus into an intracellular response
The transport of oxygen by hemoglobin
questions.e: Signal transduction is a cascade of processes that convert an extracellular stimulus into an intracellular response, allowing a cell to adapt to its environment.

questions.q: The ordered sequence of biochemical reactions inside a cell that carries out signal transduction is called the:
questions.e: Signal transduction often involves ordered sequences of biochemical reactions inside the cell, called the transduction pathway.

questions.q: Defects in signal transduction pathways are implicated in which group of diseases?
o: Diabetes, heart disease, autoimmunity, and cancer
questions.e: Many disease processes such as diabetes, heart disease, autoimmunity, and cancer arise from defects in signal transduction pathways.

questions.q: What are the four stages of signal transduction, in order?
questions.e: Signal transduction has four stages: reception, transduction, response, and termination.

questions.q: The "reception" stage of signal transduction is best described as:
o: Detection of an external signal by a cell through interaction between a messenger and a receptor
Amplification of the response inside the nucleus
questions.e: Reception (recognition) is the detection of an external signal by a cell through interaction between a messenger and a receptor.

questions.q: During the "transduction" stage, what typically happens?
o: The messenger is destroyed before binding its receptor
The receptor protein is altered, triggering a cascade of reactions known as the signal transduction pathway
questions.e: Transduction is the conversion of the signal into other signals through alteration of the receptor protein, which triggers off the signal transduction pathway.

questions.q: Which of the following is a possible outcome of the "response" stage of signal transduction?
o: Complete reversal of the original stimulus with no cellular change
Turning on a gene, activating an enzyme, or rearranging the cytoskeleton
Immediate cell death in every case
questions.e: The transduction pathway triggers a response such as turning on a gene, activating an enzyme, or rearranging the cytoskeleton; there is usually an amplification of the signal.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the mechanisms of termination of a signal transduction response?
o: Permanent covalent binding of ligand to receptor
Fall in concentration of the first messenger
questions.e: Termination occurs via falling first-messenger concentration, protein phosphatases, regeneration of G proteins, phosphodiesterases, receptor phosphorylation, uncoupling, receptor sequestration, and receptor desensitization — not permanent irreversible ligand binding.

questions.q: The voltage-dependent calcium channels found in the membrane of the T tubules are called
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Dihydropyridine receptors (DHPRs) are the voltage sensors/Ca2+ channels in the T-tubule membrane that mechanically couple to ryanodine receptors on the SR.

questions.q: When thyroxin binds to its receptor to form a hormone-receptor complex,
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Thyroxine binds an intracellular/nuclear receptor; the hormone-receptor complex acts directly on DNA to initiate gene transcription.

questions.q: Which class of molecules can cross the lipid bilayer and use intracellular receptors?
o: Only ions such as Na+ and K+
questions.e: Only lipophilic molecules — such as steroid hormones, thyroid hormones, vitamin D, and retinoic acid — can cross the lipid bilayer to use intracellular receptors.

questions.q: Which one of these is not a second messenger?
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. RGS (Regulator of G-protein Signaling) is a protein that accelerates GTP hydrolysis on G-alpha subunits — it is a signalling regulator, not a second messenger.

questions.q: Uptake of molecules by caveolae is termed
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Potocytosis is the specific term for molecule uptake via caveolae (flask-shaped membrane invaginations rich in caveolin).

questions.q: What are the three major classes of cell surface receptors?
o: Channel-linked receptors, catalytic receptors, and G protein-coupled receptors
Ionotropic, metabotropic, and structural receptors only
questions.e: The three major classes of cell surface receptors are channel-linked receptors, catalytic receptors, and G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs).

questions.q: Channel-linked receptors are notable for being:
o: Slow-acting and restricted to gene transcription
Fast-acting, transducing neurotransmitter signals directly into electrical signals
questions.e: Channel-linked receptors are fast-acting receptors that transduce chemical signals from neurotransmitters directly into electrical signals by opening or closing a channel.

questions.q: Which one of these is not a catalytic receptor?
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Adenylate (adenylyl) cyclase is an effector enzyme activated downstream of a G-protein-coupled receptor — it is not itself a catalytic (enzyme-linked) receptor.

questions.q: What happens to a catalytic receptor upon ligand occupancy?
o: It releases its ligand without any structural change
It immediately internalizes and is degraded
It dimerizes and undergoes a conformational change
It converts into a channel-linked receptor
questions.e: Ligand occupancy of catalytic receptor sites results in dimerization and a conformational change; no conformational change occurs in a single chain.

questions.q: Which catalytic receptor subtype mediates the response to atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) and NO?
questions.e: ANP and NO act on receptor guanylyl cyclases, a class of catalytic receptors.

questions.q: Which catalytic receptor subtype mediates the response to EGF, PDGF, and insulin?
questions.e: EGF, PDGF, and insulin act through receptor tyrosine kinases, a class of catalytic receptors.

questions.q: Which one of these does not act by a cytoplasmic receptor?
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Acetylcholine is hydrophilic and binds membrane-bound receptors (nicotinic/muscarinic); steroid hormones and NO act via intracellular/cytoplasmic receptors.

questions.q: What binds the alpha subunit of an inactive (resting) G protein?
questions.e: The inactive form of the G protein has GDP bound to the alpha subunit, along with beta and gamma subunits.

questions.q: When a catecholamine binds to a membrane bound receptor, the
o: hormone-receptor complex moves into the cytoplasm
second messengers appear in the cytoplasm
hormone-receptor complex moves into the nucleus
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Catecholamines act via membrane G-protein-coupled receptors, triggering intracellular second messengers (e.g. cAMP, IP3) rather than the complex itself entering the cell.

questions.q: Agonist binding to a GPCR enhances which activity of the receptor, leading to GTP loading onto the alpha subunit?
questions.e: Agonist binding to GPCRs enhances the receptor's guanine-nucleotide-exchange factor (GEF) activity, leading to GTP loading by the alpha subunit.

questions.q: After GTP loads onto the alpha subunit, what happens to the G protein?
o: It converts GTP back to GDP instantly
It dissociates into separate beta-gamma and alpha-GTP subunits
It stays bound to the receptor permanently
questions.e: The G protein is released from the receptor and dissociates into separate beta-gamma and alpha-GTP (active) subunits, which then interact with effectors.

questions.q: How does an active G protein return to its inactive state?
o: Via degradation of the beta-gamma complex
Via binding a new ligand to the receptor
Via hydrolysis of GTP to GDP by the intrinsic GTPase activity of the alpha subunit
questions.e: Active G proteins return to their inactive state upon hydrolysis of GTP to GDP by the intrinsic GTPase activity of the alpha subunit, after which alpha-GDP and beta-gamma recombine.

questions.q: What is the function of "regulator of G-protein signaling" (RGS) proteins?
o: They accelerate the rate of GTP hydrolysis by G-alpha subunits
They convert Gi proteins into Gs proteins
They slow GTP hydrolysis to prolong signaling
questions.e: RGS proteins accelerate the rate of GTP hydrolysis by G-alpha subunits, an activity dubbed GTPase-activating protein (GAP) activity.

questions.q: G proteins can be classified as stimulatory or inhibitory, denoted respectively as:
questions.e: G proteins can be stimulatory (Gs) or inhibitory (Gi), depending on their effect on the downstream effector.

questions.q: Which protein is recruited after a phosphorylated GPCR reduces its ability to respond to ligand, further desensitizing the receptor?
questions.e: Receptor phosphorylation by a kinase recruits beta-arrestin, which further desensitizes the receptor as part of switching GPCR signaling off.

questions.q: What are the three major classes of second messengers?
o: Cyclic nucleotides, IP3/DAG, and calcium ions
questions.e: There are three major classes of second messengers: cyclic nucleotides (cAMP and cGMP), IP3/DAG, and calcium ions (Ca2+).

questions.q: The enzyme responsible for conversion of ATP to cAMP is
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Adenylyl cyclase converts ATP to cAMP; phosphodiesterase later breaks cAMP down, terminating the signal.

questions.q: Which enzyme does cAMP characteristically bind and activate?
questions.e: cAMP binds and activates Protein Kinase A (PKA), a cAMP-dependent protein kinase that phosphorylates target proteins and/or alters gene transcription.

questions.q: cAMP activity is terminated when it is converted by cAMP-phosphodiesterase into:
questions.e: cAMP activity is terminated when it is converted by cAMP-phosphodiesterase to 5’-AMP.

questions.q: Which of the following is a primary messenger?
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. A primary (first) messenger is the extracellular signal — usually a hormone or neurotransmitter — that binds a cell-surface receptor. TSH fits this role. cAMP, calmodulin, and PLC-generated products (IP₃/DAG) are all second messengers generated inside the cell after receptor activation.

questions.q: IP3 and DAG are both derived from the hydrolysis of which membrane lipid, catalyzed by phospholipase C?
questions.e: IP3 and DAG are synthesized from phosphatidylinositol-4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2), which PLC hydrolyzes after GPCR-mediated activation.

questions.q: After IP3 is generated, what does it do?
o: Remains anchored in the plasma membrane
Diffuses through the cytosol and binds receptors on the endoplasmic reticulum, releasing Ca2+
Converts into DAG in the nucleus
questions.e: IP3, being water-soluble, diffuses through the cytosol to the ER, binds IP3 receptors, and causes release of Ca2+ into the cytosol.

questions.q: Unlike IP3, DAG remains where, and does what?
o: In the nucleus; binds DNA directly
In the inner layer of the plasma membrane; together with Ca2+ activates Protein Kinase C
In the ER lumen; forms calcium crystals
In the mitochondrial matrix; inhibits ATP synthase
questions.e: DAG remains in the inner layer of the plasma membrane, where together with Ca2+ (made available by IP3) it activates Protein Kinase C (PKC).

questions.q: What are the two main intracellular depots that supply Ca2+ for cell signaling?
o: The nucleus and the Golgi apparatus
The extracellular fluid and the endoplasmic reticulum
questions.e: There are two main depots of Ca2+ for the cell: the extracellular fluid and the endoplasmic reticulum (the "sarcoplasmic reticulum" in skeletal muscle).

questions.q: What is meant by "amplification" in signal transduction?
o: The signal weakens progressively at each stage
A cascading effect where the initial signal is magnified so that one messenger molecule can produce a million products
The ligand is chemically copied many times before binding
questions.e: Amplification refers to the cascading effect in signal transduction where the number of participating molecules increases at each stage, so one messenger molecule can produce a million products, often letting a small stimulus elicit a large response.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT typically classified as an excitable tissue?
questions.e: Excitable tissues capable of producing electrical signals include nerves, muscles, sensory receptors, and nerve cells. Adipose (fat) tissue is not considered an excitable tissue.

questions.q: Which part of the neuron is described as its metabolic center and contains the nucleus?
questions.e: The soma, or cell body, is the metabolic center of the neuron and houses the nucleus, which contains the genetic material as chromosomes.

questions.q: Which neuronal structure typically tapers toward its apex and receives chemical messages from other neurons?
questions.e: Dendrites are branch-like extensions from the soma that taper toward the apex and receive chemical signals from other neurons on their surfaces.

questions.q: The site of the neuron where EPSPs and IPSPs are integrated is the
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. The axon hillock is where all excitatory and inhibitory graded potentials are summed to determine if threshold is reached and an action potential fires.

questions.q: The main function of nociceptors is to sense:
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Nociceptors are free nerve endings specialized to detect noxious (potentially damaging) stimuli — mechanical, thermal, or chemical — and transmit signals that are perceived as pain.

questions.q: Functionally, which type of neuron conveys information from tissues and organs to the central nervous system?
questions.e: Sensory (afferent) neurons convey information from peripheral tissues and organs toward the central nervous system.

questions.q: Which statement about interneurons is correct?
o: They connect sensory and motor neurons, and all CNS neurons are interneurons
They are found only in the peripheral nervous system
questions.e: Interneurons provide connections between sensory and motor neurons (and among themselves); all neurons of the central nervous system, including the brain, are classified as interneurons.

questions.q: Structurally, a neuron with one short process that splits into two long axonal processes is classified as:
questions.e: Unipolar (pseudounipolar) neurons have one short process that immediately divides into two long processes, both of which are axons; they are common in the afferent division of the PNS.

questions.q: Multipolar neurons, which comprise more than 99% of human neurons, are characterized by:
o: A single process that never branches
questions.e: Multipolar neurons have multiple dendritic processes but only one axon each; they dominate the CNS and the efferent division of the PNS (e.g., spinal motor neurons, pyramidal neurons, Purkinje cells).

questions.q: The glial cells that form the blood-brain barrier are the
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Astrocyte end-feet surround brain capillaries and induce/maintain the tight junctions of the blood-brain barrier.

questions.q: Which CNS glial cell forms the myelin sheath around central axons?
questions.e: Oligodendrocytes form the myelin sheath around CNS axons and help hold nerve fibers together.

questions.q: The uptake of particulate matter by a cell is
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Phagocytosis ('cell eating') is uptake of large particulate matter; pinocytosis is uptake of fluid/solutes.

questions.q: In the peripheral nervous system, which cell forms myelin sheaths around axons?
questions.e: Schwann cells form the myelin sheaths around peripheral (PNS) axons, the counterpart of oligodendrocytes in the CNS.

questions.q: Which PNS glial cell encapsulates and supports the cell bodies of peripheral neurons?
questions.e: Satellite cells encapsulate and provide protection and support for the cell bodies of peripheral neurons, particularly within ganglia.

questions.q: The resting membrane potential of a neuron can be calculated using the
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. The GHK equation accounts for the relative permeabilities and concentrations of multiple ions (K+, Na+, Cl−) to give the overall resting membrane potential.

questions.q: A resting cell with excess negative charge inside relative to outside is described as being:
questions.e: By convention, the negative resting potential means excess negative charge inside compared to outside, and the resting cell is said to be polarized.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the three primary determinants of membrane potential?
o: Unequal ion distribution across the membrane
Membrane permeability (ion conductance) via specific channels
questions.e: Membrane potential is determined by unequal ion distribution, membrane ion permeability, and electrogenic pump activity — not by total cell volume.

questions.q: Which of these does not contribute to the generation of the resting membrane potential of a neuron?
o: Na+ influx through voltage gated Na+ channels
Active transport of Na+ out of the cell
Active transport of K+ into the cell
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Voltage-gated Na+ channels are closed at rest and only open during depolarization — they do not contribute to the resting potential.

questions.q: How much more permeable is a resting cell membrane to K+ compared with Na+?
questions.e: The resting membrane is about 50-75 times more permeable to K+ than to Na+, making K+ movement the prime determinant of the RMP.

questions.q: The equilibrium potential for a specific ion is defined as the membrane potential at which:
o: The ion channel is permanently closed
There is no net movement of that ion across the membrane
questions.e: The equilibrium potential for a given ion is the membrane potential at which there is no net movement of that ion into or out of the cell.

questions.q: The equilibrium potential of an ion can be calculated using the
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. The Nernst equation calculates the equilibrium potential for a single ion based on its concentration gradient.

questions.q: According to the values given, what is the equilibrium potential for Na+?
questions.e: The equilibrium potential for Na+ is +60 mV, reflecting the strong inward electrochemical drive on Na+ ions.

questions.q: Rate of propagation of an action potential in a neuron is increased by
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Myelination (saltatory conduction) and larger axon diameter both increase conduction velocity. Cold actually slows conduction.

questions.q: What effect does increasing the external K+ concentration have on the resting membrane potential?
o: It has no effect at all
It decreases the resting membrane potential
questions.e: Increasing the external K+ concentration decreases (makes less negative, i.e., depolarizes) the resting membrane potential, since it reduces the outward K+ gradient.

questions.q: What effect does decreasing the external Na+ concentration have on the resting membrane potential?
o: Little effect on the resting membrane potential
questions.e: Because resting Na+ permeability is low to begin with, decreasing external Na+ concentration has little effect on the resting membrane potential.

questions.q: What determines whether a stimulated nerve cell produces a graded potential versus an action potential?
o: The type of ion channel present only
questions.e: The type of response elicited — graded potential or full action potential — depends on the intensity of the stimulation relative to threshold.

questions.q: Which one of these is not a characteristic of graded potentials?
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Refractory periods are a feature of action potentials (due to Na+ channel inactivation), not graded potentials, which can summate freely without a refractory period.

questions.q: The upstroke of the SA nodal action potential is produced by opening of a channel that is:
o: Equally permeable to K⁺ and Na⁺
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Unlike ventricular myocytes, SA nodal cells lack significant fast Na⁺ channel activity. Their action potential upstroke (phase 0) is instead driven by the opening of L-type Ca²⁺ channels, producing a comparatively slower, Ca²⁺-dependent depolarization.

questions.q: What is the correct sequence of the four classic phases of an action potential?
questions.e: The correct order is: latent period, depolarization, repolarization, and finally after-hyperpolarization.

questions.q: The latent period of an action potential refers to:
o: The refractory period following the spike
The time the membrane spends fully depolarized
The isoelectric interval — time for the stimulus to travel from the point of stimulation to the recording electrode
questions.e: The latent period is the isoelectric interval — the time taken by the stimulus to travel from the point of stimulation to the recording electrode.

questions.q: What is the approximate threshold potential that must be reached to trigger the positive-feedback opening of more Na+ channels?
questions.e: Depolarization drives the interior potential from about -70 mV up to roughly -55 mV, the threshold at which more voltage-gated Na+ channels open via positive feedback.

questions.q: Which of these is not true about the neuronal action potential?
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. An action potential is not 'always depolarizing' — it involves a depolarization phase followed by repolarization (and often after-hyperpolarization). Also, action potentials do not summate (feature b in the list is the false one; note option d 'It summates' is also false, but the classically tested false statement here is 'always depolarizing').

questions.q: Repolarization of the membrane occurs primarily due to:
o: Rapid inactivation of Na+ channels plus prolonged opening of voltage-gated K+ channels
An influx of Cl- ions only
Complete closure of all ion channels
questions.e: Repolarization results from rapid inactivation of Na+ channels (reducing Na+ conductance) combined with prolonged opening of voltage-gated K+ channels, which increases K+ conductance and returns the potential toward rest.

questions.q: After-hyperpolarization occurs because:
o: Both voltage-gated and non-gated K+ channels remain open, driving the potential more negative than rest
Na+ channels remain open longer than usual
questions.e: With both voltage-gated and non-gated K+ channels open, K+ efflux continues past the resting level, making the membrane potential transiently more negative than the resting potential.

questions.q: The resting membrane potential is restored after after-hyperpolarization through which combination of mechanisms?
o: Closure of voltage-gated K+ channels, K+ efflux through non-gated channels, and restoration of ion gradients by the Na+/K+ pump
Opening of Na+ channels and closing of K+ channels only
Complete cessation of all ion movement
questions.e: The resting potential is regained through closure of voltage-gated K+ channels, continued K+ efflux through non-gated channels, and restoration of resting ion concentrations by the Na+-K+ pump.

questions.q: What effect does decreasing the external Na+ concentration have on the action potential?
o: It has no effect on the action potential
It decreases the size of the action potential
It converts the action potential into a graded potential
It increases the size of the action potential
questions.e: Decreasing the external Na+ concentration decreases the size of the action potential, since the depolarizing Na+ influx depends on the extracellular Na+ gradient.

questions.q: Once generated at one site on an axon, how is an action potential conducted along the rest of the axon?
o: By direct transmission through the myelin sheath only
By diffusion of neurotransmitter along the axon interior
By local current flow between active and adjacent inactive regions
questions.e: Action potentials are conducted along the axon by local current flow: positive charges spread from the active site toward the adjacent inactive region, driving it to threshold.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT listed as a factor influencing the speed of action potential conduction?
questions.e: Conduction velocity is influenced by fiber diameter, myelination, and temperature — not by tissue color, which has no physiological relevance here.

questions.q: Why does increasing the diameter (radius) of an axon increase its conduction velocity?
o: Because larger axons have more mitochondria
Because larger axons have fewer ion channels
Because larger axons contain more myelin automatically
Because internal resistance is inversely proportional to cross-sectional area, so larger fibers have lower resistance
questions.e: Internal resistance is inversely proportional to cross-sectional area, so larger-diameter fibers have lower internal resistance and therefore faster conduction.

questions.q: In unmyelinated axons, conduction velocity is proportional to which property of the axon diameter?
o: The square root of the diameter
The diameter has no relationship to velocity
questions.e: In unmyelinated axons, conduction velocity is proportional to the square root of the axon diameter.

questions.q: Which two effects does myelination have on axonal conduction?
o: It decreases membrane leakiness to ions and reduces membrane capacitance
It has no measurable effect on conduction
It increases membrane leakiness and increases capacitance
It only affects the resting membrane potential
questions.e: Myelination decreases the leakiness of the membrane to ions (except at the nodes of Ranvier) and greatly reduces membrane capacitance, both of which speed up conduction.

questions.q: Regular (continuous) conduction is best described as:
o: Conduction that occurs only in glial cells
A sequential, wave-like spread of the action potential occurring in unmyelinated axons
Conduction that requires no ion channels
A hopping conduction restricted to myelinated fibers
questions.e: Regular/continuous conduction is the sequential spread of the action potential as a wave, characteristic of unmyelinated axons.

questions.q: In saltatory conduction, where does depolarization occur?
o: Uniformly along the entire length of the myelinated segment
Only at the nodes of Ranvier, where membrane resistance is low
Only within the myelin sheath itself
questions.e: In saltatory conduction, depolarization occurs only at the nodes of Ranvier, where membrane resistance is low, and the action potential appears to hop from node to node.

questions.q: What is a key energetic advantage of saltatory conduction over continuous conduction?
o: It requires no ATP at all
It generates its own ATP via myelin metabolism
It saves energy by decreasing use of the Na+/K+ pump in the axonal membrane
It eliminates the need for Na+ channels
questions.e: Saltatory conduction saves energy by decreasing the use of sodium-potassium pumps across most of the axonal membrane, since ion flux is restricted mainly to the nodes of Ranvier.

questions.q: The refractory period is best defined as:
o: The time before any stimulus is applied
The period of maximal neurotransmitter release
The period when a neuron cannot generate any resting potential
The period during an action potential when the membrane\u2019s ability to respond to a second stimulus is markedly altered
questions.e: The refractory period is the period during an action potential when the ability of the membrane to respond to a second stimulus is markedly altered.

questions.q: During the absolute refractory period, a second stimulus of any strength:
o: Will always produce a second, larger action potential
Produces a delayed action potential after several seconds
Cannot produce a second action potential no matter how strong
questions.e: During the absolute refractory period, a second stimulus will not produce a second action potential no matter the strength of the stimulus.

questions.q: During the absolute refractory period
o: most of the voltage gated Na+ channels are in the inactivated state
there will be summation if a second stimulus is applied
the neuron will not respond to a second stimulus
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. During the absolute refractory period, voltage-gated Na+ channels are inactivated, so no stimulus (however strong) can trigger a new action potential.

questions.q: During the relative refractory period, a second action potential can be triggered only if:
o: No stimulus is applied at all
The membrane is first artificially hyperpolarized further
The stimulus strength is greater than threshold, decreasing gradually as the period progresses
questions.e: During the relative refractory period, a second action potential can occur only if the stimulus strength exceeds threshold, with progressively weaker stimuli sufficing as the period continues.

questions.q: Accommodation refers to a nerve\u2019s ability to:
o: Increase its resting membrane potential permanently
Adjust to a slowly increasing stimulus so that threshold is never reached and no action potential is evoked
questions.e: Accommodation is the property of a nerve by which it adjusts to a slowly increasing stimulus, so that its threshold of excitation is not attained and an action potential cannot be evoked.

questions.q: "Reception" in sensory physiology refers to:
o: The conversion of stimulus energy into a membrane potential
The ability of a receptor to absorb the energy of a stimulus
The transmission of receptor potentials to the CNS
questions.e: Reception is the ability of a receptor to absorb the energy of a stimulus, the first step in sensory processing.

questions.q: "Transduction" specifically refers to:
o: Sending signals down the axon to the synapse
Coding stimulus intensity as AP frequency
Conversion of stimulus energy into a receptor/generator potential
questions.e: Transduction is the conversion of stimulus energy into a membrane potential — a receptor potential (RP) or generator potential (GP) — that can go on to fire an action potential.

questions.q: Simple receptors, associated with the general senses, are found:
questions.e: Simple receptors and their neural pathways are associated with the general senses and are found throughout the body, as free or encapsulated nerve endings.

questions.q: Which one of these does not belong to the special senses?
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Nociception (pain) is a general (somatic) sense detected by receptors distributed throughout the body, not a special sense.

questions.q: Exteroceptors are sensitive to which of the following?
o: Internal visceral pain and hunger only
Stimuli occurring outside or on the surface of the body, such as touch, pain, temperature, vision, hearing, smell, and taste
questions.e: Exteroceptors occur at or near the skin surface and are sensitive to external stimuli such as touch, pain, temperature, vision, hearing, smell, and taste.

questions.q: Which of these sensations is not monitored by interoceptors?
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Vision is a special exteroceptive/special sense; interoceptors monitor the internal state of the body (thirst, nausea, blood pressure, fatigue).

questions.q: Proprioceptors respond to stimuli occurring in which structures?
o: Skeletal muscles, tendons, ligaments, inner ear, and joints
questions.e: Proprioceptors respond to stimuli in skeletal muscles, tendons, ligaments, the inner ear, and joints, providing information about body position and movement.

questions.q: Which receptor type responds to physical force such as pressure and stretch?
questions.e: Mechanoreceptors respond to physical force, including pressure (touch or blood pressure) and stretch.

questions.q: Which receptor type responds to dissolved chemicals in taste and smell, as well as internal chemistry changes like O2, CO2, and H+ levels?
questions.e: Chemoreceptors respond to dissolved chemicals during taste and smell sensations, as well as to changes in internal body chemistry such as O2, CO2, or H+ variations.

questions.q: Sensory transduction results in which immediate cellular event?
o: Opening or closing of ion channels, leading to a change in membrane potential
Direct release of hormones into the bloodstream
questions.e: In sensory transduction, interaction between the stimulus and the receptor results in opening or closing of ion channels, leading to a graded change in membrane potential called a receptor or generator potential.

questions.q: The adequate stimulus of nociceptors is
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Nociceptors respond to noxious/tissue-damaging stimuli, generating the sensation of pain — the best-fit answer among the options given.

questions.q: Sensory "adaptation" refers to:
o: A permanent loss of receptor function
A conversion of receptor potentials into resting potentials
A decrease in responsiveness of receptors to a uniformly maintained stimulus of constant intensity
An increase in receptor sensitivity over time under constant stimulation
questions.e: Adaptation is a decrease in the responsiveness of receptors to a uniformly maintained stimulus of constant intensity, seen as declining AP frequency and a subjectively weaker stimulus over time.

questions.q: Phasic receptors, such as the Pacinian corpuscle, are characterized by:
o: Quick adaptation to stimuli such as touch, odor, temperature, and pressure
questions.e: Phasic receptors adapt quickly and are typically associated with touch, odor, temperature, and pressure sensations; the Pacinian corpuscle is a classic example.

questions.q: Tonic receptors, such as proprioceptors and pain receptors, are characterized by:
o: Slow adaptation, maintaining a sustained response to ongoing stimuli
questions.e: Tonic receptors adapt slowly, allowing sustained signaling — important for proprioceptors, blood pressure receptors, and pain receptors that must report ongoing conditions.

questions.q: The concept of "modality" in sensory coding refers to:
o: The anatomical size of the receptor
The specific type of sensation, encoded by labeled lines — specific fibers carrying specific modalities
The intensity of the stimulus only
questions.e: Modality refers to the type of sensation experienced (pain, touch, pressure, etc.), encoded via labeled lines — specific nerve fibers dedicated to transmitting specific modalities, decoded by where their tracts terminate in the CNS.

questions.q: Stimulus intensity is coded by
o: activation of different types of receptors
frequency of APs fired by the sensory neuron
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Intensity is encoded by population/spatial coding (recruitment of more sensory units) and rate/frequency coding (more APs per second). Activation of different receptor types encodes modality, not intensity.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the five main functions of muscle tissue?
questions.e: Muscles maintain posture, stabilize joints, produce movement, generate heat, and guard entrances/exits. Red blood cell production occurs in bone marrow, not muscle tissue.

questions.q: True or False: Muscle tissue has both the ability to contract and to conduct electrical impulses.
questions.e: TRUE. Muscle tissue is specialized to both contract and conduct electrical impulses, making it unique among body tissues.

questions.q: Functionally, muscles are classified into which two types?
questions.e: The functional classification divides muscles into voluntary (conscious control) and involuntary (not under conscious control). Striated vs smooth is the structural classification.

questions.q: Which type of muscle is described as striated AND involuntary?
questions.e: Cardiac muscle is striated and involuntary, found in the heart wall. Skeletal muscle is striated voluntary; smooth muscle is non-striated involuntary.

questions.q: True or False: Smooth muscle is primarily found in tubular organs.
questions.e: TRUE. Smooth (involuntary) muscle is found primarily in the walls of tubular organs such as the gut, blood vessels, and urinary tract.

questions.q: The connective tissue that encloses the sarcolemma of an individual muscle fiber is called
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Endomysium surrounds individual muscle fibers; perimysium surrounds fascicles (bundles); epimysium surrounds the whole muscle.

questions.q: The connective tissue surrounding individual fascicles within a skeletal muscle is:
questions.e: Perimysium surrounds each fascicle (bundle of muscle fibers). Epimysium covers the whole muscle and endomysium covers individual muscle cells.

questions.q: True or False: Skeletal muscle fibers are branched and mononucleated.
questions.e: FALSE. Skeletal muscle fibers are elongated, UNBRANCHED, cylindrical, and MULTINUCLEATED. Branching is a feature of cardiac muscle fibers.

questions.q: Where are the nuclei located in a skeletal muscle fiber?
o: In the center of the cell
In the peripheral aspect just under the sarcolemma
questions.e: Nuclei of skeletal muscle fibers are located peripherally, just beneath the sarcolemma. In cardiac and smooth muscle, nuclei are centrally placed.

questions.q: The plasma membrane of a skeletal muscle cell is specifically called the:
questions.e: The sarcolemma is the specialized plasma membrane of a muscle fiber. The sarcoplasmic reticulum is the modified smooth ER inside the cell.

questions.q: The PRIMARY function of the sarcoplasmic reticulum in skeletal muscle is to:
questions.e: The primary function of the sarcoplasmic reticulum is to store Ca2+ and release them during excitation-contraction coupling to trigger contraction.

questions.q: True or False: T-tubules are extensions of the sarcolemma and contain extracellular fluid.
questions.e: TRUE. T-tubules are invaginations of the sarcolemma and their lumen contains ECF, as they are extensions of the cell surface membrane.

questions.q: The function of T-tubules in skeletal muscle is to:
o: Conduct impulses from the surface into the cell to the SR
questions.e: T-tubules conduct electrical impulses (action potentials) from the cell surface deep into the cell, specifically reaching the sarcoplasmic reticulum to trigger Ca2+ release.

questions.q: Triads in skeletal muscle consist of:
o: Two T-tubules and one terminal cistern
One T-tubule flanked by two terminal cisterns
questions.e: A triad = ONE T-tubule flanked by TWO terminal cisterns (enlarged ends of the SR). Triads are located at the A-I band junction.

questions.q: The cytoplasm of a muscle cell containing mitochondria and enzymes is called the:
questions.e: Sarcoplasm is the cytoplasm of a muscle cell. It surrounds the myofibrils and contains mitochondria, enzymes, glycogen, and other organelles.

questions.q: The A-band in a sarcomere corresponds to:
o: The region containing only the Z-line
The H-zone of thin filaments only
The zone where thick filaments are present
questions.e: The A-band (anisotropic) is the dark band spanning the entire length of the thick (myosin) filaments, including overlap regions with thin filaments.

questions.q: The H-band within the A-band represents:
o: The zone of maximum overlap between thick and thin filaments
The region containing only thin filaments
The zone where there is NO overlap between thick and thin filaments
questions.e: The H-band is the lighter region within the A-band where NO overlap exists between thick and thin filaments — only the central portions of thick filaments are present here.

questions.q: True or False: During muscle contraction, both the thick and thin filaments shorten in length.
questions.e: FALSE. According to the sliding filament theory, filament lengths do NOT change. The thin filaments slide past the thick filaments, shortening the sarcomere while filament lengths remain constant.

questions.q: The functional contractile unit of skeletal muscle is the:
questions.e: The sarcomere — the unit from one Z-line to the next — is the fundamental contractile unit of a muscle fiber, containing a complete set of overlapping thick and thin filaments.

questions.q: The dark Z-line in the sarcomere connects:
questions.e: The Z-line (Z-disc) connects adjacent thin filaments and marks the boundaries of each sarcomere. Thick filaments are connected at the M-line.

questions.q: How many thin myofilaments surround each thick myofilament in a skeletal muscle fiber?
questions.e: Each thick myofilament is surrounded by 6 thin myofilaments in a hexagonal arrangement. Conversely, each thin filament is surrounded by 3 thick filaments.

questions.q: Titin (connectin) in the sarcomere functions primarily as:
o: A blocker of actin binding sites
A molecular spring providing passive elasticity
questions.e: Titin is a giant protein spanning from the Z-disc to the M-line, acting as molecular springs and serving as the MAIN source of passive elasticity in muscle.

questions.q: True or False: The I-band contains only thin (actin) filaments.
questions.e: TRUE. The I-band (isotropic) is the light band containing ONLY thin filaments. The Z-line bisects each I-band.

questions.q: Thick myofilaments are primarily composed of which protein?
questions.e: Thick filaments are composed of myosin. Each myosin molecule has a tail forming the filament core and two heads (cross-bridges) that project outward and interact with actin.

questions.q: The myosin cross-bridge (head) possesses all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.e: The myosin head has an ATP-binding site (ATPase), an actin-binding site, and a hinge. Calcium binding occurs at Troponin C on the THIN filament, NOT on the myosin head.

questions.q: Thin myofilaments are composed of which combination of proteins?
questions.e: Thin filaments contain three proteins: actin (double helical backbone), troponin (regulatory complex), and tropomyosin (long filament blocking binding sites at rest).

questions.q: Myosin binding sites on the actin filament are exposed after
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Ca2+ binding to troponin C causes a conformational change that shifts tropomyosin, exposing the myosin-binding sites on actin.

questions.q: Which troponin subunit binds to calcium ions?
questions.e: Troponin C (TnC) is the calcium-binding subunit. TnT binds tropomyosin, TnI binds actin to anchor the complex, and TnC binds Ca2+ to initiate the conformational change leading to contraction.

questions.q: At rest, the tropomyosin molecule is held in place by
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Troponin binds tropomyosin and, at rest (low Ca2+), holds it over the myosin-binding sites on actin.

questions.q: Each thin myofilament consists of two chains of actin arranged as a:
questions.e: Each thin myofilament contains two chains of spherical actin molecules wound into a double helix, with myosin binding sites present on the actin molecules.

questions.q: The rapid rise and fall in force produced by a muscle fiber after a single action potential is
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. A single action potential produces a single twitch — a brief rise and fall in tension.

questions.q: True or False: Depolarization in a skeletal muscle fiber starts at the motor end plate.
questions.e: TRUE. Depolarization begins at the motor end plate (neuromuscular junction) where acetylcholine from the motor neuron binds to receptors on the sarcolemma.

questions.q: Voltage-dependent calcium channels in the T-tubule membrane that sense the action potential are called:
questions.e: Dihydropyridine receptors (DHPRs) are voltage-sensitive channels in the T-tubule membrane that detect the action potential and mechanically open ryanodine receptors on the SR.

questions.q: Ryanodine receptors (RyRs) are located on the:
questions.e: Ryanodine receptors are on the sarcoplasmic reticulum membrane. When DHPRs change conformation, they mechanically open RyRs, releasing Ca2+ from the SR into the sarcoplasm.

questions.q: Excitation-contraction coupling is defined as the process by which:
o: ATP is hydrolyzed by myosin ATPase
Depolarization of the muscle fiber initiates contraction
The sarcomere shortens during a power stroke
Actin binds to myosin to form cross-bridges
questions.e: Excitation-contraction coupling links electrical excitation (depolarization) of the muscle fiber membrane to the mechanical response (contraction) of the muscle.

questions.q: The FIRST step in cross-bridge cycling is:
questions.e: ATP hydrolysis is the first step: ATP binds to the myosin cross-bridge and is hydrolyzed to ADP + Pi. This energizes the myosin head and increases its affinity for actin.

questions.q: During the power stroke, the thin filament moves toward:
questions.e: The rotation of the myosin head (power stroke) pulls the thin filament toward the CENTER of the sarcomere (toward the M-line), shortening the sarcomere.

questions.q: Which molecule is released from the myosin head at the START of the power stroke?
questions.e: Release of inorganic phosphate (Pi) TRIGGERS the power stroke. ADP is released DURING the power stroke while the myosin head remains attached to actin.

questions.q: True or False: The myosin head detaches from actin when a new ATP molecule binds to the myosin ATP-binding site.
questions.e: TRUE. Binding of a new ATP molecule decreases myosin's affinity for actin, causing detachment. Without ATP (as in rigor mortis), myosin permanently stays attached to actin.

questions.q: During the power stroke, which nucleotide is released from the myosin head?
questions.e: ADP is released from the myosin head DURING the power stroke. The cross-bridge stays attached to actin throughout the power stroke until a new ATP binds.

questions.q: The cross-bridge cycle continues as long as:
o: Troponin is in its resting conformation
Tropomyosin is blocking actin binding sites
questions.e: Cross-bridge cycling continues as long as sarcoplasmic Ca2+ remains elevated. When Ca2+ is pumped back into the SR, troponin-tropomyosin re-blocks actin, and contraction ceases.

questions.q: According to the sliding filament theory, during contraction, which of the following DECREASES?
questions.e: The sarcomere width (distance between Z-lines) DECREASES as Z-lines are drawn closer together. The lengths of thick and thin filaments themselves remain UNCHANGED.

questions.q: True or False: The sliding filament mechanism requires both sufficient calcium ions and sufficient ATP.
questions.e: TRUE. Calcium is needed to unblock actin binding sites via troponin-tropomyosin, and ATP is needed to energize the myosin head and allow cross-bridge detachment.

questions.q: Muscle relaxation occurs when calcium is actively pumped back into the SR by:
questions.e: The Ca2+-ATPase (SERCA pump) actively transports Ca2+ back into the SR using ATP, lowering sarcoplasmic Ca2+ and allowing tropomyosin to re-block actin binding sites.

questions.q: When sarcoplasmic Ca2+ falls below 10^-7 M during relaxation, tropomyosin:
o: Moves to expose myosin binding sites on actin
Returns to block the myosin binding sites on actin
questions.e: When Ca2+ dissociates from troponin C, tropomyosin returns to its blocking position on actin, preventing further cross-bridge formation and halting contraction.

questions.q: The immediate energy source for ALL muscle contractions is:
questions.e: ATP is the only immediate and direct energy source for muscle contraction. All other energy sources (creatine phosphate, glycogen, cellular respiration) function by REGENERATING ATP.

questions.q: Unassisted ATP stores in muscle can sustain contraction for approximately:
questions.e: ATP stores alone can sustain contraction for only about 3 seconds. Other energy systems rapidly replenish ATP to continue contraction beyond this.

questions.q: Creatine phosphate regenerates ATP through which reaction?
o: Creatine phosphate + ADP to creatine + ATP
Creatine + ATP to creatine phosphate + ADP
Creatine phosphate + ATP to creatine + ADP
questions.e: The reaction is: Creatine phosphate + ADP → Creatine + ATP, catalyzed by creatine phosphotransferase. This reversible reaction quickly regenerates ATP.

questions.q: The creatine phosphate energy system is called alactic anaerobic because it:
o: Produces lactic acid and requires oxygen
Requires oxygen but produces no lactate
Neither produces lactate nor requires oxygen
Produces lactate but does not require oxygen
questions.e: The phosphagen (creatine phosphate) system is alactic anaerobic — it does not produce lactic acid AND does not require oxygen. It sustains contraction for 5-8 seconds.

questions.q: After creatine phosphate depletion, the next energy system to provide ATP is:
questions.e: After creatine phosphate is depleted, glycolysis using stored glycogen provides the next ATP source, sustaining contraction for up to about 1 minute.

questions.q: True or False: Skeletal muscle fibers contain approximately 1% glycogen.
questions.e: TRUE. Skeletal muscle fibers contain about 1% glycogen. Glycogenolysis produces glucose-1-phosphate which enters the glycolytic pathway to regenerate ATP.

questions.q: Which of these is not true during oxidative phosphorylation
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Pyruvic acid is produced during glycolysis and consumed (converted to Acetyl-CoA) before oxidative phosphorylation — it is not produced during this process.

questions.q: Rigor mortis occurs because of:
o: Depletion of ATP causing permanent cross-bridge formation
Rapid degradation of actin filaments after death
questions.e: Rigor mortis results from depletion of ATP (and creatine phosphate) after death. Without ATP, myosin cannot detach from actin, causing permanent cross-bridge formation and extreme rigidity.

questions.q: Cellular respiration for ATP production primarily uses which substrates?
questions.e: Oxidative metabolism primarily uses glucose and free fatty acids. It is the slowest but most efficient ATP-generating system, sustaining prolonged muscle activity.

questions.q: In isometric contraction, which of the following is TRUE?
o: The muscle generates force without changing length
The muscle lengthens under an external load
The muscle shortens with constant load
questions.e: Isometric contraction occurs when muscle generates force but does NOT shorten — for example, attempting to lift an immovable object. No visible movement occurs.

questions.q: True or False: In concentric isotonic contraction, the force generated by the muscle always exceeds its maximum force.
questions.e: FALSE. In concentric contraction, force generated EXCEEDS the load (so muscle shortens), but this force is always SUBMAXIMAL. Maximum force is typically generated during eccentric contractions.

questions.q: During a biceps curl, the DOWNWARD movement of the dumbbell represents:
questions.e: The downward movement is an eccentric contraction — the muscle generates force but the external load exceeds this force, so the muscle LENGTHENS while contracting.

questions.q: Series Elastic Elements (SEE) in muscle include:
o: Muscle membranes parallel to contractile elements
questions.e: Series Elastic Elements are in series with the contractile elements and include titin and tendons. They lengthen slightly during contraction and allow a contracted muscle to stretch past L0.

questions.q: Parallel Elastic Elements (PEE) in muscle produce tension when the muscle is:
questions.e: PEE (provided by muscle membranes, endomysium, perimysium, and epimysium) produce tension when a muscle is PASSIVELY STRETCHED past its resting length L0.

questions.q: A motor unit consists of:
o: All motor neurons controlling a single muscle
A motor neuron and ALL the muscle fibers it innervates
A single sarcomere with all its cross-bridges
One muscle fiber and all its sarcomeres
questions.e: A motor unit is a single motor neuron plus ALL skeletal muscle fibers it innervates. All fibers in a motor unit contract simultaneously when the neuron fires.

questions.q: True or False: A single motor unit can contain a mixture of Type I, Type IIa, and Type IIb muscle fibers.
questions.e: FALSE. A single motor unit contains only ONE type of muscle fiber. Most skeletal muscles contain mixtures of fiber types, but individual motor units are fiber-type specific.

questions.q: The force generated by a motor unit is determined by all of the following EXCEPT:
o: Number of muscle fibers in the unit
Number of cross-bridges attached to actin
questions.e: Force depends on number of fibers, cell size, initial fiber length, and number of cross-bridges. Myoglobin content relates to fatigue resistance and oxygen storage, not force generation directly.

questions.q: The minimum stimulus that results in a muscle twitch is called the:
